units.blurb: Rival kings, reunification under Mentuhotep II, and the classic age of the 12th Dynasty (c. 2160–1650 BC).

topics.title: The Nile Valley and the Delta
topics.short: Egypt was the Nile valley, a strip of farmland rarely more than 20 km wide, and the fan-shaped Delta, between deserts.
topics.trouble: Students picture Egypt as a broad country. Nearly everyone lived in the valley and the Delta; the deserts held mines, quarries, oases and trade routes.

topics.title: The Inundation
topics.short: Summer rains in Ethiopia raised the Nile each year, flooding the valley and leaving silt; the height of the flood decided the harvest.
topics.trouble: Students think the flood came from rain in Egypt. It came from monsoon rains far south, on the Ethiopian highlands; Egypt itself has almost no rain.

topics.title: The Two Lands and the Nomes
topics.short: Egyptians called their country the Two Lands, Upper (south) and Lower (north) Egypt, divided into provinces called nomes.
topics.trouble: Upper and Lower are reversed from what a map suggests: Upper Egypt is the south, upstream.

topics.title: Sources for Egyptian History
topics.short: Historians use monuments and inscriptions, papyri and ostraca, archaeology, foreign records and later Greek writers, each with its own biases.
topics.trouble: Students take royal inscriptions at face value. Kings recorded victories, not defeats; every source has a point of view.

topics.title: Kingdoms and Intermediate Periods
topics.short: Modern historians divide Egyptian history into kingdoms (times of one strong state) and intermediate periods (times of division).
topics.trouble: Students think the Egyptians used these names. "Old Kingdom" and "Intermediate Period" are modern labels.

topics.title: King Lists
topics.short: Ancient king lists, like the Palermo Stone, the Turin Canon and the lists at Abydos and Saqqara, give kings in order, but leave some out.
topics.trouble: Students treat a king list as complete. The Abydos list skips rulers the later kings rejected, such as Hatshepsut and the Amarna kings.

topics.title: Manetho's Dynasties
topics.short: Manetho, an Egyptian priest of the early 3rd century BC, wrote a history in Greek that grouped the kings into the 30 dynasties we still use.
topics.trouble: Students think a dynasty is always one family. Manetho's dynasties sometimes change with the capital rather than the bloodline, and some overlap in time.

topics.title: Dating by Regnal Years
topics.short: Egyptians dated events by the year of the king's reign ("Year 5 of His Majesty"), so dates have to be added up king by king.
topics.trouble: Students expect a continuous era like BC and AD. Each reign restarted the count, and overlaps (co-regencies) make adding up hard.

topics.title: Astronomical Dates
topics.short: A few texts record the rising of the star Sirius or the phases of the moon, which can tie reigns to absolute dates; scholars still debate how to read them.
topics.trouble: Students take astronomical dates as exact. Where the observation was made, and how the calendar worked, change the result by decades.

topics.title: Radiocarbon and Egyptian Dates
topics.short: Radiocarbon dating of plant remains from dated contexts largely agrees with the standard chronology and is most useful for the earliest periods.
topics.trouble: Students think radiocarbon gives one exact year. It gives a range, often several decades wide.

topics.title: How Sure Are the Dates?
topics.short: Dates are fixed from 664 BC on; before that they are approximate, uncertain by decades in the New Kingdom and by a century or more in the Old Kingdom.
topics.trouble: Students quote early dates as exact years. A date like 2589 BC for Khufu is a best estimate; this course uses Shaw's Oxford History (2000) and writes "c.".

topics.title: Before the Kings: Badari and Naqada
topics.short: Farming villages appeared along the Nile in the 5th millennium BC; the Naqada culture spread across Egypt and grew into chiefdoms.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptian civilization appeared suddenly. It grew over many centuries of village farming and trade.

topics.title: The First Writing
topics.short: Small labels from a tomb at Abydos (tomb U-j, c. 3200 BC) carry some of the earliest known Egyptian writing.
topics.trouble: Students assume Egyptians borrowed writing from Mesopotamia. Writing appeared in both about the same time; whether one influenced the other is debated.

topics.title: The Joining of the Two Lands
topics.short: Around 3000 BC the Nile valley and the Delta came under one king; the Narmer Palette shows King Narmer in the white crown on one side and the red crown on the other.
topics.trouble: Students treat the palette as a news photo of one battle. It is a ceremonial object; unification was probably a long process.

topics.title: The First Dynasties
topics.short: Kings of Dynasties 1 and 2 ruled from Memphis, were buried at Abydos, and built the tools of the state: writing, taxes and royal titles.
topics.trouble: Students think the pyramids came first. Two dynasties of mud-brick tombs came before them.

topics.title: Djoser and the Step Pyramid
topics.short: Djoser of the 3rd Dynasty built the first large stone building, the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, credited to his official Imhotep.
topics.trouble: Students think the Step Pyramid was built as six steps from the start. It grew from a flat mastaba through several changes of plan.

topics.title: Sneferu, Khufu and the True Pyramid
topics.short: In the 4th Dynasty, Sneferu built the first true pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur, and Khufu the Great Pyramid at Giza.
topics.trouble: Students credit the Great Pyramid with being the first pyramid. Sneferu built three before it, learning from mistakes.

topics.title: The State That Built the Pyramids
topics.short: Pyramids needed an organized state: a vizier, scribes, taxes in grain and labor, quarries, boats and a fed, housed workforce.
topics.trouble: The old idea of huge gangs of slaves does not fit the evidence. Workers' towns, bakeries and tombs at Giza point to organized, fed Egyptian crews.

topics.title: The Sun Kings and the Pyramid Texts
topics.short: Kings of the 5th Dynasty built sun temples for Ra, and Unas, the last of them, had the first Pyramid Texts carved in his tomb.
topics.trouble: Students think the Pyramid Texts were carved in the Great Pyramid. The Great Pyramid has no inscriptions inside; the texts begin with Unas, about two centuries later.

topics.title: The 6th Dynasty and the Provinces
topics.short: Under the 6th Dynasty, provincial governors grew richer and more independent; officials like Weni and Harkhuf left autobiographies of their careers.
topics.trouble: Students imagine all power stayed with the king. Over time, the governors of the nomes built their own power bases.

topics.title: Why Did the Old Kingdom End?
topics.short: Historians debate the causes: a weaker central government, very long reigns, and perhaps low Nile floods and a drier climate.
topics.trouble: Students look for a single cause. Most historians see several working together, and they disagree about how much climate mattered.

topics.title: The First Intermediate Period
topics.short: After the Old Kingdom, rival dynasties ruled from Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south.
topics.trouble: Later Egyptian texts paint this time as total chaos. Many local towns did well; the picture of disaster is partly propaganda of the later kings.

topics.title: Mentuhotep II Reunites Egypt
topics.short: Mentuhotep II of Thebes defeated the Herakleopolitan kings and reunited Egypt (c. 2055 BC), beginning the Middle Kingdom.
topics.trouble: Students expect a new kingdom to start with a new dynasty. Mentuhotep II was already a king of the 11th Dynasty.

topics.title: The 12th Dynasty
topics.short: Amenemhat I founded the 12th Dynasty and a new capital, Itjtawy; its kings, named Amenemhat and Senusret, ruled about two centuries.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the repeated names. Number them (Senusret I, II, III) and tie each to a deed.

topics.title: Senusret III and Nubia
topics.short: Senusret III built a chain of forts at the Second Cataract, fixed the southern border, and reduced the power of provincial governors.
topics.trouble: Students place the border at Aswan for all of history. In the Middle Kingdom Egypt pushed south to the Second Cataract.

topics.title: The Classic Age
topics.short: The Middle Kingdom was the classic age of Egyptian literature, such as the Tale of Sinuhe and the teaching texts, written in Middle Egyptian.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptian writing was only religious or royal. Middle Kingdom scribes wrote stories, poems and advice.

topics.title: The Hyksos
topics.short: The Hyksos, rulers of western Asian origin, governed the north from Avaris as the 15th Dynasty (c. 1650–1550 BC).
topics.trouble: Students picture a sudden invasion by a horde. Archaeology shows people from western Asia living in the Delta for generations before Hyksos kings took power.

topics.title: The Kingdom of Kush at Kerma
topics.short: South of Egypt, the kingdom of Kush, centered at Kerma, grew strong and allied with the Hyksos.
topics.trouble: Students see Nubia only as Egypt's colony. Kerma was a powerful kingdom with its own culture.

topics.title: The Theban War
topics.short: Theban kings Seqenenre Tao and Kamose fought the Hyksos, and Ahmose took Avaris and drove them out (c. 1550 BC).
topics.trouble: Students think the war was quick. It took at least three Theban kings.

topics.title: Ahmose and the New Kingdom
topics.short: Ahmose founded the 18th Dynasty; his successors pushed into the Levant and Nubia and built Egypt's empire.
topics.trouble: Students date the empire to Ramesses II. It was built mostly by the early 18th Dynasty kings.

topics.title: Hatshepsut
topics.short: Hatshepsut ruled first as regent for Thutmose III and then as king (c. 1473–1458 BC), building at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari.
topics.trouble: Students repeat that her images were destroyed right after her death in anger. Most were removed late in Thutmose III's reign, perhaps for reasons of succession.

topics.title: Thutmose III and Megiddo
topics.short: Thutmose III won the battle of Megiddo and led many campaigns into the Levant, making Egypt the leading power of the region.
topics.trouble: Students mix up Megiddo (Thutmose III) and Kadesh (Ramesses II).

topics.title: Amenhotep III and the Amarna Letters
topics.short: Amenhotep III ruled a rich and peaceful empire; his letters with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and others survive in the Amarna archive.
topics.trouble: Students think the Amarna letters were written in Egyptian. They are clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic language of the day.

topics.title: Akhenaten and Amarna
topics.short: Akhenaten made the Aten, the sun disk, the center of worship, closed temples of other gods and built a new capital at Amarna.
topics.trouble: Students call Akhenaten's religion simple monotheism. Scholars debate the word; the king himself kept a special place between the Aten and the people.

topics.title: Tutankhamun and the Restoration
topics.short: Tutankhamun, Ay and Horemheb brought back the old gods and left Amarna; later kings erased the Amarna kings from their lists.
topics.trouble: Students think Tutankhamun was a great ruler. He was a young king whose fame comes from his tomb; Horemheb was the stronger figure.

topics.title: Ramesses II
topics.short: Ramesses II of the 19th Dynasty reigned 66 years (1279–1213 BC), built more than any other king and moved his capital to Pi-Ramesses.
topics.trouble: Students credit Ramesses with every monument bearing his name. He also carved his name on older buildings.

topics.title: Kadesh and the Peace Treaty
topics.short: At Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; years later the two powers signed a peace treaty.
topics.trouble: Students read Ramesses' temple reliefs as proof of a great victory. Hittite records and the outcome suggest a draw.

topics.title: Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples
topics.short: Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples; in his reign came the first known strike, by the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sea Peoples were one nation. They were a mix of groups on the move, and their origins are debated.

topics.title: The End of the New Kingdom
topics.short: Under the later Ramesses, Egypt lost its empire, tombs were robbed, and the high priests of Amun at Thebes grew powerful.
topics.trouble: Students expect a sudden fall. The New Kingdom wound down over a century.

topics.title: A Divided Egypt
topics.short: In the Third Intermediate Period, kings at Tanis and then Libyan dynasties ruled the north while the priests of Amun held Thebes.
topics.trouble: Students think "intermediate" means nothing happened. Art, temples and trade went on; power was shared out.

topics.title: The Kushite Kings
topics.short: Kings from Kush, such as Piye and Taharqo, conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty until the Assyrians drove them out.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians always ruled Nubia. Here Nubian kings ruled Egypt, and saw themselves as true heirs of the pharaohs.

topics.title: The Saite Revival
topics.short: Psamtek I became king at Sais in 664 BC and had reunited Egypt by 656 BC; the 26th Dynasty copied Old Kingdom art and welcomed Greek traders and soldiers.
topics.trouble: Students skip the Late Period as a time of decline. The Saite kings ran a strong, wealthy state.

topics.title: Persian Rule
topics.short: In 525 BC Cambyses of Persia conquered Egypt; Persian kings ruled it as the 27th Dynasty until 404 BC.
topics.trouble: Students repeat Herodotus's stories of Cambyses' cruelty. Egyptian records of his reign paint a milder picture, and scholars weigh the two.

topics.title: The Last Native Kings
topics.short: Egyptian kings ruled again from 404 BC until Persia returned in 343 BC; Nectanebo II was the last native pharaoh.
topics.trouble: Students think Cleopatra was the last Egyptian pharaoh. She was Macedonian Greek by family; Nectanebo II was the last native-born king.

topics.title: Alexander in Egypt
topics.short: Alexander the Great took Egypt from Persia in 332 BC, visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa and founded Alexandria.
topics.trouble: Students think Alexander fought a great battle for Egypt. The Persian governor gave it up without a fight.

topics.title: The Ptolemies and Alexandria
topics.short: Ptolemy I and his heirs ruled from Alexandria, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse, as Greek kings and as pharaohs.
topics.trouble: Students think the Ptolemies ignored Egyptian religion. They built and rebuilt great Egyptian temples, like Edfu and Philae.

topics.title: Cleopatra VII
topics.short: Cleopatra VII, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony, lost to Octavian at Actium (31 BC); after her death in 30 BC Egypt became Roman.
topics.trouble: Students take the Roman picture of Cleopatra as fact. Most surviving accounts were written by her enemies or long after.

topics.title: Roman Egypt
topics.short: Rome ruled Egypt as a special province, and its grain fed the city of Rome.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptian culture ended with the Romans. Temples were still built and hieroglyphs carved for centuries.

topics.title: Christian and Byzantine Egypt
topics.short: Christianity spread through Egypt; monks like Antony and Pachomius founded monastic life, and Coptic became the Christian Egyptians' written language.
topics.trouble: Students date the end of Egyptian religion to one year. Old temples closed over a long time; Philae was among the last.

topics.title: The Arab Conquest
topics.short: Arab armies under Amr ibn al-As took the fortress of Babylon in AD 641 and then Alexandria, ending Byzantine rule.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians changed language and religion at once. Coptic and Christianity remained widespread for centuries.

topics.title: Divine Kingship and the Titulary
topics.short: The king was Horus on earth and son of Ra, standing between the gods and the people; his five names expressed this role.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians saw the living king as all-powerful. The office was divine; the king could still be criticized, plotted against, or fail.

topics.title: The Vizier and the Officials
topics.short: A vizier ran the government with scribes and officials who counted harvests, collected taxes and kept records.
topics.trouble: Students imagine the king did everything. Most governing was done by trained officials.

topics.title: An Economy Without Coins
topics.short: Until the Late Period Egyptians did not use coins; they traded goods valued in units of copper (deben) or grain, and wages were paid in bread and beer.
topics.trouble: Students assume money meant coins. Egyptians priced things in deben without needing coins.

topics.title: The People of Egypt
topics.short: Most Egyptians were farmers; above them were craftsmen, scribes, priests and officials; there were servants and some slaves, especially war captives.
topics.trouble: Students picture a land of slaves or a land of equals. Egypt was a ranked society; slavery existed but did not build the pyramids.

topics.title: Deir el-Medina, the Workmen's Village
topics.short: The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs lived at Deir el-Medina; thousands of their notes on pottery and stone survive.
topics.trouble: Students think we know only about kings. Deir el-Medina gives the names, quarrels, debts and jokes of ordinary workers.

topics.title: Women in Ancient Egypt
topics.short: Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court and inherit, though few held office.
topics.trouble: Students assume ancient women had no rights. Egyptian women had more legal rights than in many ancient societies, though men held most offices.

topics.title: The Army
topics.short: Egypt's army grew from local levies into a standing army of the New Kingdom, with chariots and foreign troops.
topics.trouble: Students think chariots were always Egyptian. Horses and chariots came into Egypt around the Second Intermediate Period.

topics.title: Egypt and Nubia
topics.short: For three thousand years Egypt traded with, fought and ruled parts of Nubia, and Nubian kings once ruled Egypt.
topics.trouble: Students see Nubia only through Egyptian eyes. Nubian kingdoms (Kerma, Napata, Meroë) had their own long history.

topics.title: Egypt and the Near East
topics.short: Egypt traded with Byblos for cedar, ruled parts of Canaan, and dealt with Mitanni, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon and Persia.
topics.trouble: Students treat Egypt as cut off by deserts. It was part of a busy world of trade and diplomacy.

topics.title: Egypt and the Bible: What Scholars Debate
topics.short: Historians debate how stories of Joseph and the Exodus relate to Egyptian evidence; many identify Shishak with Shoshenq I, though some doubt it.
topics.trouble: Students expect a simple yes or no. Scholars weigh the evidence differently, and the question remains open; here we lay out the main positions.
